extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in personality psychology and measurement of humor styles
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and measurement instruments for individual differences in humor use (humor 'styles'), including questionnaires and the four principal styles (affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, self-defeating). Summarizes item content, scoring formats, reliability notes, and associated outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of Humor Questionnaire (original)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally a 22-item questionnaire broken into three categories (M-items: reactive to humor and implicit messages; L-items: attitude towards humorous people and situations; E-items: openness to expression of amusement) with item responses on a 1-4 scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: M-item: 'when I go to the movies I prefer to know ahead what type of story it is'; L-item: 'fun is aimed at hurting another'; E-item: 'do you ever laugh so hard it hurts?'. M- and L-items use 1=total agreement to 4=total disagreement; E-items use 1=very seldom to 4=very often. Note dimensionality problems: some items overlap categories. Revised versions improved M and L internal consistency (in the .60s–.70s) but E-items showed poor internal consistency and were dropped from later uses; M-items fed into the Situational Humor Response and L-items into the Humor Coping Scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coping Humor Scale (CHS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 7-item self-report scale assessing the extent participants use humor to cope with stress. Responses use a 1–4 scale (1=strongly disagree to 4=strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported internal consistency alphas range around .60–.70; 12-week test–retest reliability ~.80. Unique for strong self–observer agreement: participants' self-ratings correlate with friends' ratings on similar content. Use to quantify humor-as-coping rather than type or frequency of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Humor Response Questionnaire (SHRQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrument composed of 18 situational items (from everyday to anxiety-inducing events) plus 3 non-situational items, measuring how often an individual smiles, laughs, or shows amusement in different situations. Responses use a 1–5 scale (1='I would not have been particularly amused' to 5='I would have laughed heartily').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three non-situational items assess desirability of easily amused friends, how much one's humor changes by situation, and self-rating of likelihood to laugh. Psychometrics: alpha coefficients .70–.83 across groups; one-month test–retest alpha ~.70. Low correlation (.04) with Crowne–Marlowe social desirability scale, suggesting relative freedom from social desirability bias. SHRQ measures frequency/reactivity to humor but ignores type/style of humor used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidimensional Sense of Humor Scale (MSHS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developed from several earlier scales, originally 124 statements reduced to 29 items with responses on a 1–5 scale (1=strongly disagree to 5=strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 29 items load onto four factors: (1) humor production / humor for social uses, (2) coping humor / adaptive humor, (3) humor appreciation, and (4) attitude toward humor. The reduced scale reported high reliability (alpha ≈ .92). Example item types: 'I use humor to entertain my friends', 'uses of humor help me master difficult situations', 'I like a good joke', 'people who tell jokes are a pain in the neck'. Use when assessing multiple facets of 'sense of humor' including production, appreciation, coping, and attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor Styles Questionnaire (HSQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 32-item self-report inventory (responses 1='totally disagree' to 7='totally agree') designed to measure individual differences in how people use humor. It maps two orthogonal dimensions (1) whether humor is used to enhance the self vs. enhance relationships and (2) whether humor is benevolent vs. detrimental, producing four styles: affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, and self-defeating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to link humor usage styles with health, well-being, and interpersonal outcomes. Psychometric notes: original (German) version internal consistencies > .77 for scales; translated versions show variable alphas (e.g., aggressive scale as low as .55 in some studies, self-enhancing up to .89). Translation and cultural differences can alter item functioning; aggressive scale often shows lowest internal consistency. HSQ items — include positively- and negatively-worded items and example items such as 'I enjoy making people laugh' and style-specific items listed under each style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliative humor (HSQ style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humor style used to enhance one's relationships with others in a benevolent, positive manner. Characterized by spontaneous joking, witty banter, charming/amusing others, easing tension, and laughing with others; not used at one's own expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes and associations: linked to initiating friendships, reduced victimization from bullying, increased group cohesiveness and workplace creativity, higher explicit and implicit self-esteem, greater psychological well-being and emotional stability, decreased depressive symptoms and anxiety; associated personality traits include higher extraversion and openness. HSQ example items: reversed items such as 'I don't often joke around with my friends' and 'I rarely make other people laugh by telling funny stories about myself.' Use as a positive, relationship-enhancing humor metric (contrast with self-defeating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-enhancing humor (HSQ style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humor style reflecting a good-natured attitude toward life and the ability to laugh at oneself and life's absurdities in a constructive, non-detrimental way; functions as coping or emotion-regulation (finding the silver lining).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated outcomes: lower depressive symptoms, greater creativity, reduced workplace stress, higher self-esteem and optimism, greater psychological well-being, lower anxiety; personality correlates include higher extraversion and openness, lower neuroticism. HSQ example items: 'If I am feeling upset or unhappy I usually try to think of something funny about the situation to make myself feel better.' and 'Even when I'm by myself, I'm often amused by the absurdities of life.' Use to measure adaptive, intrapersonal use of humor for emotion regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive humor (HSQ style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A potentially detrimental humor style characterized by sarcasm, put-downs, teasing, ridicule, criticism, and humor at others' expense, sometimes expressing prejudices (e.g., racism, sexism). Often disregards the impact on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated outcomes and traits: higher neuroticism, lower agreeableness and conscientiousness, higher hostility and general aggression; males tend to use more aggressive humor. HSQ example items: 'When telling jokes or saying funny things, I am usually not very concerned about how other people are taking it.' and reversed items like 'People are never offended or hurt by my sense of humor.' Use as an interpersonal, potentially harmful humor metric; interpret relative to social costs and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defeating humor (HSQ style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humor style involving self-disparaging humor used to gain approval from others; the individual becomes the 'butt' of jokes and may use humor defensively to hide negative feelings (a form of denial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated outcomes: increased depressive symptoms, higher anxiety and psychiatric symptoms, lower self-esteem, lower psychological well-being and intimacy, higher bullying victimization; personality correlates include higher neuroticism and lower agreeableness and conscientiousness. HSQ example items: 'I often try to make people like or accept me more by saying something funny about my own weaknesses, blunders, or faults.' and 'If I am having problems or feeling unhappy, I often cover it up by joking around, so that even my closest friends don't know how I really feel.' Use to identify maladaptive interpersonal humor patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants and contextual moderators of humor styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that influence what people find humorous and how they use humor, including culture, age, political orientation, and social context; humor usage shows some situational variability though tends to be relatively stable as a personality characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution when comparing across cultures and languages—differences in norms and translations can affect questionnaire responses. Consider social context when interpreting style scores (people may modulate style by situation). The article notes a lack of reliable research distinguishing healthy vs. unhealthy humor in some cases due to subjectivity; thus contextual and cultural moderators should be considered when applying these measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric considerations for humor measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: General measurement-quality issues raised across scales: internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), test–retest reliability, translation/cultural validity, item dimensionality, and susceptibility to social desirability biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from article: Sense of Humor Questionnaire had overlap/dimensionality problems and E-items with poor internal consistency; CHS alphas ~.60–.70 and 12-week test–retest ~.80; SHRQ alphas .70–.83 and low correlation with social desirability; HSQ original alphas >.77 but translated versions vary widely (aggressive scale often low). When using these instruments, report scale alphas, consider confirmatory factor analyses when translating, be aware of reversed items, and interpret low alpha scales (especially aggressive) with caution.
